text:
A suspension bridge carries traffic on a deck, but the deck does not carry the full span’s weight directly to the ground. Instead, it passes much of that weight upward through vertical or nearly vertical hangers to large main cables. The main cables drape over tall towers and extend to anchorages beyond them. Together, these parts provide a continuous load path: every force applied to the bridge must ultimately be balanced by forces from the ground supporting and restraining it.

The process begins where a vehicle’s wheels, a pedestrian’s feet, or the deck’s own weight press downward. The deck slab transfers these loads into supporting beams and a longitudinal stiffening system, often a truss or a streamlined steel box. This structure spreads concentrated loads over a larger length of bridge, rather than letting one small area carry everything. It also resists bending and twisting, helping the roadway remain reasonably smooth when traffic occupies only part of the span.

At regular intervals, hangers connect the deck’s supporting structure to the main cables overhead. A hanger works in tension: the deck pulls down on its lower end, while the main cable pulls up on its upper end. This stretching force supports the deck. The hanger, in turn, pulls downward on the main cable at its attachment point. Although many bridges use vertical hangers, some use inclined ones; either arrangement transfers deck loads through tension into the main suspension system.

The main cables also work primarily in tension. Their curved shape is essential because a flexible cable cannot support a transverse load by resisting bending as a beam does. At each loaded point, the tension forces acting along the cable have components that balance the downward pull of the hangers. Across the span, these forces carry the loads toward the towers and anchorages. A shallower cable sag generally requires greater horizontal tension for the same span and load, which strongly influences the bridge’s proportions.

Where the cables pass over the towers, they press downward through supports called saddles. The towers carry this force mainly as compression, transferring it through their legs to foundations below. Horizontal cable forces on opposite sides of a tower substantially balance under suitable loading, but unequal loading and other effects can also make towers bend. Their foundations spread the resulting forces into competent soil or rock through large footings, piles, or other deep foundation systems.

At the ends of a conventional suspension bridge, massive anchorages resist the main cables’ strong inward and upward pull. These anchorages transfer that pull into the earth through their weight, their connection to rock, and resistance from the surrounding ground. Thus, the towers and anchorages perform different but complementary jobs: the towers mainly deliver vertical compression, while the anchorages secure the cable tension. Wind, braking, temperature changes, and earthquakes add lateral, longitudinal, or changing forces, handled by the deck, bracing, bearings, towers, and foundations. The bridge remains stable because this whole connected system provides balanced routes for loads to reach the ground while allowing controlled movement.
